Command: A priest shall not shave his head bald or trim his beard's corners
Summary: The command: A priest shall not shave his head bald or trim his beard's corners (Leviticus 21:5). Priests were not to make baldness on their heads, shave the corners of their beards, or cut their flesh, as mourning rites of the nations.
Commandment: A priest shall not shave his head bald or trim his beard's corners.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The priest's holiness had a cost: because he handled holy things, his contact with death was restricted beyond the people's. The high priest's restriction was stricter still (Leviticus 21:10-12). The New Testament's great High Priest, by contrast, touches the dead and raises them — the restriction pointed to a holiness he embodies differently (Hebrews 4:14-16).
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: they shall be holy unto their God, and not profane the name of their God (Leviticus 21:6).
Function: Priests were not to make baldness on their heads, shave the corners of their beards, or cut their flesh, as the nations did in mourning — a ceremonial law against borrowed rites. Its goal was to keep the priesthood visibly distinct from the mourning customs of the peoples around Israel, who marked grief on the body. The evil was importing pagan mourning into God's priesthood, letting the nations' rites shape holy men. It restrained that by forbidding the marks themselves, so the priest's body never preached another religion.
